title: Orbits, satellites and the lines on the globe
source: DeepKids Combined. Covers NIOS Class 5, Lesson 11 'Solar System and Earth' (the planets and the Earth; planets and satellites; phases of the Moon; natural and man-made satellites; latitude and longitude; time zones). No textbook needed.
summary: A satellite stays up because it is always falling and always missing the Earth. Your child rolls a marble round a plate to see what keeps something moving in a circle, and works out why the Moon always shows us the same face and which phase rises at which hour. They meet the moons of other worlds and the satellites people have launched, including India's first, Aryabhata. Then they draw the lines of latitude and longitude on a ball, find their own latitude from the Pole Star, learn how a carpenter's clock solved the longitude problem, and see why India has one clock time even though the Sun rises nearly two hours earlier in Arunachal than in Kutch.
builds_on: In Class 3 your child met the Sun, the planets, the Moon and the stars. In Class 4 they kept a Moon diary, made eclipses with a lamp and a bead, and read shadows. In Class 4 (Day, night, seasons and rhythms of nature) they spun a globe to see day and night. In Class 5 (Day, night, seasons and rhythms of nature) they will also see how the Earth's tilt and orbit make seasons. Later, in middle school, they will meet gravity and the life of stars in more detail.
goals: By the end your child can explain the difference between a planet and a satellite, and give examples of natural and artificial satellites.
By the end your child can explain that an orbit is falling round and round, and why satellites don't fall down.
By the end your child can predict when each phase of the Moon rises, and explain why we always see the same face.
By the end your child can find a place using latitude and longitude, and estimate their own latitude from the Pole Star.
By the end your child can explain time zones (15 degrees for each hour) and Indian Standard Time, and argue for or against a second time zone for India.

words: satellite
anything that orbits a planet. The Moon is a natural satellite, and a weather satellite is an artificial one.
orbit
the curved path of something falling round and round a bigger body
gravity
the pull that every object has on every other. The Earth's gravity keeps the Moon and satellites in orbit.
equator
the imaginary line round the middle of the Earth, halfway between the poles
latitude
how far north or south of the equator a place is, measured in degrees
longitude
how far east or west of the prime meridian a place is, measured in degrees
prime meridian
the line of 0 degrees longitude, which runs through Greenwich in London
tropic
one of two lines of latitude (about 23.4 degrees north and south) where the Sun can be overhead
time zone
a region that keeps the same clock time
chronometer
a very accurate clock that keeps time even on a rolling ship
light-year
the distance light travels in a year, about 9.5 lakh crore kilometres
space debris
dead satellites and broken pieces of rockets left circling the Earth

days.title: Planets and the things that circle them
days.goal: Recall Class 4 and sort the solar system into planets, dwarf planets and satellites.

steps.title: From the Moon diary to the Moon's path
steps.do: Recall Class 4. Ask: 'Last year you kept a Moon diary and made an eclipse with a lamp and a bead. What did you find?' Good answers: 'The Moon rises about 50 minutes later each night.' 'A solar eclipse is the Moon's shadow on the Earth.' Ask: 'What is the Moon doing that makes it rise later each night?' (Moving along its orbit round the Earth.) Say: 'This year we find out what an orbit really is.'

steps.title: Story: The Satellite That Kept Falling
steps.do: Read the story aloud. Stop after the satellite's radio goes quiet and ask: 'If it has no engine and nobody can talk to it, why doesn't it fall down?' Let your child guess, then finish the story and ask the story questions.

steps.title: Planet or satellite?
steps.do: Say: 'A planet goes round a star. A satellite goes round a planet.' Name these, and your child says planet, dwarf planet or satellite: Earth, the Moon, Pluto, Titan, Mars, Phobos, Jupiter, the International Space Station, the satellite Aryabhata, Ceres. Ask: 'The Earth goes round the Sun. Is it a satellite?' (We call it a planet, because it goes round a star. The name matters less than the movement.)

steps.title: How far is far?
steps.do: Say: 'Light is the fastest thing there is. In one second it could go round the Earth more than seven times. It reaches the Moon in just over 1 second, the Sun in about 8 minutes, Neptune in about 4 hours, and the next nearest star in more than 4 years. The distance light goes in a year is called a light-year.' Ask: 'When you look at a star that is 100 light-years away, are you seeing it as it is now?' (No. You see it as it was 100 years ago. The light left it before your great-grandparents were born.)

steps.title: One line
steps.do: Your child writes in their notebook: 'A satellite is ____. My favourite satellite is ____ because ____.'

days.title: Falling round the world
days.goal: Feel that an orbit is a fall that keeps missing.

steps.title: Throwing harder
steps.do: Throw a soft ball gently across the room onto a bed: it curves down and lands near. Throw it a little harder: it lands further away. Ask: 'What if you could throw it so hard that the ground curved away underneath it before it landed?'

steps.title: Newton's cannon
steps.do: Draw a big circle (the Earth) with a mountain on top and a cannon on it. Draw three shots: a slow one that lands close, a faster one that lands far, and a very fast one that falls all the way round and comes back. Say: 'Isaac Newton drew a picture like this about 340 years ago. A satellite is falling all the time. But it is moving sideways so fast, about 8 kilometres every second for a low satellite, that the Earth's curve falls away underneath it. It keeps falling and keeps missing.' Ask: 'Why do astronauts float in the space station?' (They and the station are falling together.)

steps.title: Marble on a plate
steps.do: Do Experiment e1. Before the marble reaches the gap, your child says where they think it will go, and why.

steps.title: Why we always see the same face
steps.do: Put a chair in the middle of the room (the Earth). Your child is the Moon and walks once round the chair, always facing it. Ask a helper: 'Did the Moon spin?' (Yes, once, because they faced every wall of the room in turn.) Say: 'The Moon spins exactly once each time it goes round us, so the same face always points at the Earth. Long ago, the Earth's pull slowed the Moon's spin down to match.'

steps.title: Katherine Johnson checks the numbers
steps.do: Tell your child about Voice v4, Katherine Johnson, whose hand calculations of orbits an astronaut trusted with his life. Ask the voice question.

steps.title: Orbit in a sentence
steps.do: Ask: 'What two things make an orbit?' Good answer: 'A pull towards the middle, and a fast movement sideways.'

need: a paper plate, scissors and a marble

days.title: Which Moon rises when?
days.goal: Use the lamp-and-ball model to predict when each phase rises and sets.

steps.title: What do you remember?
steps.do: Ask your child to draw the eight phases in order from Amavasya to Amavasya, from memory or from the Class 4 Moon diary. Correct gently with the model if needed.

steps.title: The Moon clock
steps.do: Do Experiment e2. Your child turns slowly in front of the lamp while you hold the ball at each of the four main phase positions. They fill in a table with four columns: phase, rises, highest, sets.

steps.title: Two Moon months
steps.do: Say: 'The Moon goes round the Earth in about 27 and a third days. But from one full Moon to the next takes about 29 and a half days. Why the extra two days?' Use the lamp and ball: walk the Earth a little way round the lamp while the Moon goes round once. Show that the Moon has to go a little further to line up with the Sun again. Ask: 'So which month do calendars use?' (The 29 and a half day one, from phase to phase.)

steps.title: Core worksheet
steps.do: Your child does the core worksheet ws1. Keep the plate, the marble and the lamp handy, so they can test any answer they are unsure of.

need: a white ball on a stick

days.title: Moons and machines
days.goal: Meet natural and artificial satellites, and the junk around the Earth.

steps.title: Moons of other worlds
steps.do: Say: 'Our solar system has hundreds of known moons. Jupiter's moon Europa is thought to have a salty ocean under its ice. Saturn's moon Titan has rivers and lakes, but they are liquid methane, not water, under a thick orange sky. Mars has two tiny potato-shaped moons, Phobos and Deimos.' Ask: 'Which would you visit, and why?'

steps.title: What do artificial satellites do?
steps.do: Ask your child to guess what satellites do before you tell. Weather satellites, like India's INSAT satellites, watch clouds and cyclones. Communication satellites carry TV and phone signals. Navigation satellites, like India's NavIC and the American GPS, tell your phone where it is. Earth-watching satellites map crops, forests and floods. Telescopes in space look far away. India's first satellite, Aryabhata, went up in 1975 and was pictured on the old two-rupee note. Ask: 'Which of these did you use today without knowing?'

steps.title: Spot a satellite
steps.do: Look up on a free satellite-tracking website or app when the International Space Station will pass over your town. It is seen in the hour or two after sunset or before sunrise. Watch from a balcony, terrace or window that faces the right part of the sky. It looks like a bright, steady star that moves smoothly across the sky in a few minutes, with no blinking lights. If there is no pass this week, watch after dusk for any slow, steady moving dot. Many of them are satellites catching sunlight.

steps.title: Space junk
steps.do: Tell your child about Voice v2, Donald Kessler and space debris. Ask the voice question and talk about who should clean up.

need: a phone or computer to check satellite passes

days.title: Lines of latitude
days.goal: Learn the equator, tropics and poles, and find your latitude from the Pole Star.

steps.title: Where are you?
steps.do: Ask: 'If you had to tell a friend on the other side of the world exactly where your house is on Earth, with no names of places, how would you do it?' Let them invent a system.

steps.title: Draw the grid on a ball
steps.do: Do Activity a1: draw the equator, tropics, poles and a few lines of latitude and longitude on a ball or balloon, and mark India.

steps.title: Find your latitude from the Pole Star
steps.do: Do Activity a2 after dark on a clear night, or plan it for the next clear night.

steps.title: The Tropic of Cancer across India
steps.do: Say: 'The Tropic of Cancer, at about 23.4 degrees north, crosses eight Indian states: Gujarat, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, West Bengal, Tripura and Mizoram. South of it, the noon Sun is straight overhead on two days a year. Remember Zero Shadow Day from Class 4. North of it, the Sun is never overhead.' Find the line on a map of India. Ask: 'Is your home north or south of it?'

need: a clear night and a view low to the north

days.title: The longitude problem
days.goal: Find out why east and west were so hard to measure, and how a clock solved it.

steps.title: Latitude results
steps.do: Look at last night's Pole Star measurement. Compare with your town's real latitude (look it up). Ask: 'How close were you? What made it hard?'

steps.title: A clock that saved sailors
steps.do: Tell your child about Voice v1, John Harrison and the longitude problem. Explain the idea: the Earth turns 15 degrees every hour. If you know the time at home and the time where you are (from the noon Sun), the difference tells you how far east or west you have gone. Ask the voice question.

steps.title: Coordinate treasure hunt
steps.do: Do Activity a3 with an atlas or online map. Your child finds the six coordinates, then writes the coordinates of your own town.

steps.title: Who drew the zero line?
steps.do: Say: 'Latitude has a natural zero: the equator, halfway between the poles. Longitude has no natural zero. In 1884, at a meeting in Washington, people from 25 countries chose the line through Greenwich, in London, because most ships already used British sea charts. France did not vote for it and kept its own line through Paris for many more years.' Ask: 'If India had chosen, where might the zero line have gone?' (Ujjain was the zero line in many old Indian astronomy books.)

need: an atlas or a map app

days.title: One country, one clock?
days.goal: Understand time zones and weigh up the debate about Indian Standard Time.

steps.title: Calling a cousin
steps.do: Ask: 'If it is 8 pm here, what time is it for someone in London? In New York? In Tokyo?' Look it up together, or call a relative abroad and ask. (London is 4 and a half or 5 and a half hours behind India, depending on the season.)

steps.title: Torch, globe and clocks
steps.do: Do Experiment e3 with stickers for India, London, New York and Tokyo.

steps.title: Indian Standard Time
steps.do: Say: 'India stretches from about 68 degrees east to about 97 degrees east. That is about 29 degrees, nearly two hours of the Sun's time. But we use one clock, Indian Standard Time. It is set by the line at 82.5 degrees east, near Mirzapur in Uttar Pradesh, and is 5 and a half hours ahead of Greenwich.' Ask: 'In June the Sun rises around 4:30 am in parts of Arunachal Pradesh and around 6 am in western Gujarat. What problems might that cause?'

steps.title: Should India have two time zones?
steps.do: Tell your child about Voice v3, the time-zone debate. Ask the voice question and have a short debate: your child argues one side, you argue the other, then swap.

steps.title: Stretch worksheet
steps.do: Your child does the stretch worksheet ws2, using the 15-degrees-an-hour rule.

days.title: Grid Quest, check and teach it back
days.goal: Put it all together and teach it back.

steps.title: Grid Quest
steps.do: Play the card game g1. Check each place card in the atlas. For question cards, ask for a reason as well as the answer.

steps.title: Challenge worksheet
steps.do: Your child tries the challenge worksheet ws3. For the time-difference question, let them use the globe and torch to work it out.

steps.title: End check
steps.do: Ask the check questions aloud. For any muddled answer, go back to the marble, the lamp or the gridded ball and test it again.

steps.title: Teach it back
steps.do: Your child teaches a family member with the marble, the plate and the gridded ball: what an orbit is, what satellites do, how latitude and longitude find a place, and why the clock is different in London. The listener asks one hard question. Then finish the project, the postcard from orbit.

need: the paper plate and the marble

cats: set by nature (the Earth's shape, spin and tilt)

opts: it is the centre of the Earth
Britain had the most ships and sea charts using it

sections.p: Fishers on the Kerala coast use NavIC on their phones to find their way and get cyclone warnings. Some older fishers still read the stars, the waves and the birds. Thankamma says the satellite is all a fisher needs. Her grandmother says the old knowledge still matters. Pick one side and give a reason. Then give one good point for the other side.

Thousands of new satellites are being launched to bring the internet everywhere. Astronomers say the satellites leave bright streaks on telescope pictures of the sky. Who should decide what goes into orbit? Give your view and one fair point for the other side.

experiments.title: Marble on a plate
experiments.question: What keeps something moving in a circle?
need: a paper plate with a raised rim
a smooth, flat floor or table
steps: Put the plate flat on the floor. Roll the marble fast round the inside of the rim. Watch it go round in a circle.
Ask: 'What is stopping the marble from going straight?' (The rim pushes it inwards all the time.)
A grown-up cuts away about a quarter of the rim with scissors.
Roll the marble round the rim again. Watch where it goes when it reaches the gap.
Try it three times, because one try can be a fluke.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'When the marble reaches the gap, will it fly straight outwards, keep curving, or go straight on in the direction it was moving? Why do you think so?'
experiments.observe: At the gap the marble rolls off in a straight line, in the direction it was moving at that moment. It does not fly straight outwards and it does not keep curving.
experiments.why: Anything moving keeps going in a straight line unless something pushes or pulls it. The rim pushes the marble inwards, so its path bends into a circle. For the Moon and satellites, gravity does the rim's job. It pulls them towards the Earth all the time, bending their straight path into an orbit. If gravity vanished, the Moon would go off in a straight line.
experiments.safety: An adult uses the scissors. Pick up the marble afterwards, so nobody slips on it and small children don't put it in their mouth.

experiments.title: The Moon clock
experiments.question: At what time of day does each phase of the Moon rise?
need: a white ball on a stick (the Moon)
steps: Your child stands facing the lamp. Say: 'Your nose is your home. Facing the lamp is noon. Facing away is midnight. You will turn to your left. When the lamp disappears on your right, that is sunset. When it appears on your left, that is sunrise.'

Hold the ball in the full Moon position (opposite the lamp, a little above the head). Your child turns slowly. Ask: 'When does the full Moon come into view on your left (rise)?' (At sunset.) 'When is it highest?' (Midnight.)
Repeat with the ball at first quarter (a quarter turn to the left of the lamp), at new Moon (between your child and the lamp) and at last quarter (a quarter turn to the right of the lamp).
Write a table with four columns: phase, rises, highest, sets.
experiments.predict: Ask your child to guess first: 'Can you see a full Moon at noon? When does the half Moon rise?'
experiments.observe: The full Moon rises at sunset and sets at sunrise. The new Moon rises and sets with the Sun, so it is lost in the glare. The first quarter rises around noon and is high at sunset. The last quarter rises around midnight and is high at sunrise.
experiments.why: Each phase is a different angle between the Sun, Earth and Moon, so each phase is on a different side of the Earth from the Sun and rises at a different time. That is why you can see a half Moon in the afternoon sky, and why the full Moon is up all night.

experiments.title: Torch, globe and clocks
experiments.question: Why is it a different time in different places?
need: 4 stickers: India, London, New York, Tokyo
a sheet of paper and pen
steps: Stick the four labels in the right places (a globe or atlas helps).
Shine the torch at the ball from one side. Turn the ball so the torch shines straight at India: noon in India.
Ask: 'Where is it sunset? Midnight? Sunrise?' (Tokyo is in the afternoon, London in the early morning, New York in the night.)
Turn the ball anticlockwise, as seen from above the North Pole, a little at a time. Count how many hours of turning it takes until London reaches noon (about 4 and a half to 5 and a half).
experiments.predict: Ask: 'When it is noon in India, is it morning or evening in London?'
experiments.observe: Places east of India, like Tokyo, reach noon earlier. Places west of India, like London and New York, reach it later. Only half the globe is lit at any moment.
experiments.why: The Earth turns 360 degrees in 24 hours, which is 15 degrees every hour. A place 15 degrees east of you sees noon one hour earlier. Countries set their clocks to match their part of the turning world, giving us time zones.
experiments.safety: Don't shine the torch into anyone's eyes.

activities.title: Draw the grid on a ball
need: a strip of paper to measure halfway
steps: Mark a North Pole and a South Pole at the top and bottom.
Draw the equator round the middle, halfway between them. Label it 0°.
Draw the Tropic of Cancer a quarter of the way from the equator to the North Pole (about 23°), and the Tropic of Capricorn the same distance south.
Draw a line from pole to pole: the prime meridian (0° longitude). Draw three more from pole to pole, a quarter of the way round each time: 90°E, 180°, 90°W.
Mark India. The Tropic of Cancer runs through its middle, and India lies between about 68°E and 97°E, so draw it a little to the west of the 90°E line.
activities.outcome: A home-made globe with the main lines of latitude and longitude, and India in its place.

activities.title: Find your latitude from the Pole Star
need: a balcony, terrace or window with a view low to the north
a free star-map app, if buildings or haze hide the stars
steps: Find the Saptarishi and follow the two pointer stars to Dhruva Tara, the Pole Star, as in Class 3. The Saptarishi is easiest to see in the evening from February to July.
Stretch your arm out straight and make a fist. One fist at arm's length covers about 10 degrees of sky.
Starting from the horizon straight below the Pole Star, stack fists one above the other until you reach it. Count them.
Multiply by 10. That is roughly your latitude in degrees north.
Write it down, and tomorrow compare it with the real latitude of your town.
activities.outcome: Your child measures their own latitude with nothing but a fist and a star, as sailors did for centuries. In South India the Pole Star is low, only about 8 to 13 degrees up, so buildings or haze may hide it. If so, use the star-map app to see where it would be, and measure the height of the buildings in fists instead.

activities.title: Coordinate treasure hunt
need: an atlas or a map app that shows latitude and longitude
steps: Give your child these coordinates and ask them to find each place: 12.3°N 76.6°E (Mysuru), 9.9°N 76.3°E (Kochi), 25.6°N 85.1°E (Patna, near Aryabhata's Kusumapura), 51.5°N 0.0° (Greenwich), 0.0° 78.5°W (near Quito, on the equator) and 90°N (the North Pole).
Then your child writes the coordinates of your own town, and of a place a relative lives.
Ask: 'Which places are east of Greenwich and which west? North of the equator or south?'
activities.outcome: Your child can read and write a place's latitude and longitude.

project.title: A postcard from orbit
steps: Imagine you are a satellite, like Aryabhata, orbiting the Earth.
On a card, draw the Earth from space with the line between day and night across it.
On the back, write a postcard home: what kind of satellite you are, how fast you are going, why you don't fall, and what time it is in three places you can see below.
Add your home's latitude and longitude as the 'address'.
project.outcome: A postcard that shows your child understands orbits, satellites, latitude, longitude and time zones.

game.title: Grid Quest
need: an atlas or map app to check
rules: Cut out and shuffle the cards. Place them face down.
Take turns to turn one over and read it aloud.
For a place card, everyone guesses the place. The closest guess wins the card. Check in an atlas.
For a question card, the reader's left-hand neighbour answers first. Right answer wins the card.
Most cards at the end wins.

big: Space is shared by everyone. Should anyone be allowed to fill it with satellites?

challenge.q: 'There is no gravity in space. That is why astronauts float.' Is that right?
challenge.hint: At the height of the space station, the Earth's gravity is about nine-tenths as strong as on the ground. Astronauts float because they and the station are falling round the Earth together. You would float the same way inside a falling lift. Without gravity, the station would fly off in a straight line.

challenge.q: 'You can see the Great Wall of China from the Moon.' Can you?
challenge.hint: No. From the Moon, the whole Earth looks about the size of a coin held at arm's length, so no building can be seen. Even from the space station, the Wall is very hard to see, because it is narrow and the same colour as the land around it. Astronauts, including China's first, Yang Liwei, have said they could not see it.

challenge.q: 'Greenwich is at 0° because it is the middle of the world.' Is it?
challenge.hint: There is no natural middle for east and west. The line was chosen at an 1884 meeting in Washington, mainly because most of the world's ships already used British charts. France kept using Paris for decades. Any line of longitude would do as a starting line.

perspectives.view: For over a hundred years, many tea gardens in Assam have kept 'chai bagaan time', an hour ahead of IST, to make use of the early sunrise. Ask: who should a clock be set for, the capital or the people who live by the light?

Many astronomers worry that thousands of new internet satellites leave bright streaks across telescope pictures and radio signals that drown out faint ones from space. Ask: is a dark, quiet sky a shared treasure, like clean air? Who speaks for it?

perspectives.who: Fishers on the coasts of Kerala and Tamil Nadu
perspectives.view: Many fishers now use NavIC or GPS on their phones to find fishing spots and to get cyclone warnings sent by satellite. Some older fishers still read the stars, the waves and the birds. Ask: what might each kind of knowledge notice that the other misses?

voices.idea: A self-taught carpenter and clockmaker, he spent over 40 years building sea clocks accurate enough to keep home time on a rolling ship. On a 1761–1762 test voyage to Jamaica, his watch H4 lost only about 5 seconds in 81 days. Comparing the clock's home time with local noon gave a ship's longitude.
voices.then: The Board of Longitude, run by astronomers and mathematicians, favoured a method using the Moon's position among the stars, and doubted a self-taught clockmaker. They kept asking for more tests and never gave him the full prize. In 1773, with King George III's support, Parliament paid him most of the money.
voices.now: Harrison's idea won. The marine chronometer was the standard way to find longitude until radio and satellites took over. His first four sea clocks are at the Royal Observatory in Greenwich.
voices.ask: The experts favoured the method that used their own skills. Why might experts find it hard to accept a solution from an outsider? How should a new idea be tested fairly?

voices.idea: In 1978 he and Burton Cour-Palais warned that if there were enough objects in low orbit, collisions would make pieces that cause more collisions, in a chain reaction that could make some orbits unusable. This is now called the Kessler syndrome.
voices.then: Many thought it was a far-off worry.
voices.now: Today, tens of thousands of tracked pieces of debris circle the Earth, and the space station sometimes has to move to dodge them. Scientists agree debris is a serious problem. They debate how close we are to a runaway chain reaction, and how to clean up. India's own 2019 anti-satellite test, Mission Shakti, also made debris, though nearly all of it has since fallen and burned up.
voices.ask: Space has no owner and no rubbish collector. Who should pay to clean up a mess that many countries made?

voices.who: Scientists at India's National Physical Laboratory, who keep Indian Standard Time, and the people who disagree with them
voices.idea: In 2018, scientists at CSIR–National Physical Laboratory, which keeps India's official time, published a proposal for two time zones: one for most of India and one, an hour ahead, for the Northeast, to match the early sunrise there and save electricity.
voices.then: Others, including government committees over the years, have argued that one time zone keeps the country together and avoids confusion for trains, flights and offices. China, which is even wider, uses a single time zone.
voices.now: India still has one time zone. The argument is not about the science, which everyone agrees on (the Sun rises nearly two hours earlier in the far east), but about what matters most.
voices.ask: Should clocks follow the Sun where people live, or be the same for the whole country? Who gains and who loses each way?

voices.idea: She was a mathematician in a group of Black women 'computers' at NASA's Langley centre, and she worked out by hand the paths of early American spaceflights. In 1962, before John Glenn became the first American to orbit the Earth, he asked for her to check the electronic computer's numbers herself. She did, and he flew. She later worked on calculations for the Apollo Moon missions.
voices.then: At first she worked in a segregated building. Like the other women, she was long left out of the public story, and the flights' engineers got the credit.
voices.now: Her work is now honoured: she received the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2015, and a NASA building is named after her. Her story reached the public through the 2016 book and film Hidden Figures.
voices.ask: John Glenn trusted a person's careful checking over a new machine. When should we trust a machine's answer, and when should a human check it?

check.q: What is the difference between a planet and a satellite?
check.a: A planet goes round a star. A satellite goes round a planet.

check.q: Why doesn't a satellite fall to Earth?
check.a: It is falling, but it is moving sideways so fast that the Earth curves away beneath it, so it keeps missing.

check.q: Give two uses of artificial satellites.
check.a: For example: weather forecasting, phones and TV, navigation (NavIC, GPS), mapping crops and floods, telescopes.

check.q: When does a full Moon rise?
What is latitude? How could you find yours at night?
check.a: How far north or south of the equator you are. Measure how high the Pole Star is above the horizon.
The line of 0 degrees longitude, through Greenwich in London.

check.q: Why do places have different times?
check.a: The Earth turns 15 degrees every hour, so places to the east see the Sun earlier.

check.q: Where is Indian Standard Time set, and how far ahead of Greenwich is it?
check.a: At 82.5°E, near Mirzapur. It is 5 hours 30 minutes ahead of Greenwich.

story.title: The Satellite That Kept Falling
text: I was born in a shed in Bangalore. Not a grand laboratory, just a set of low buildings in an industrial area at Peenya, where young engineers in short-sleeved shirts worked late into the night, drinking strong coffee out of steel tumblers, building me piece by piece. I had twenty-six sides, like a cut jewel, and almost every side was covered in tiny blue solar cells. I weighed about as much as five grown men. They called me Aryabhata, after the astronomer who said, fifteen hundred years ago, that the Earth turns.

In April 1975, they packed me up and flew me to a launch site far away in the Soviet Union, because India did not yet have a rocket big enough. On the nineteenth, the rocket roared, and I was shaken and squeezed and flung upwards, and then, quite suddenly, everything was silent, and I was alone above the world.
I want to tell you what I saw.

The Earth was not below me, the way a floor is below you. It was beside me, enormous, filling half of everything, blue and white and brown and very bright. And there was a line across it. On one side was day, and on the other side was night, and the line between them was soft, like the edge of a shadow on a wall. As I went round, I saw that line move. Very slowly, it swept across the land. I watched it cross Arunachal and Assam, and the forests there lit up gold, and it was morning. Then it crossed the plains of the Ganga, and then, almost two hours later, it reached the salt flats of Kutch. The whole of India had one clock, but the Sun did not care about clocks. It woke the east first.

I went round the world in about an hour and a half. That meant I saw a sunrise and a sunset roughly every hour and a half: fifteen sunrises a day. I counted them. It was the kind of thing you could count, up there, with nothing to do but go round.

At first I was busy. I talked to the engineers below by radio, sending them numbers about the Sun and the sky and the air at the top of the world. They were so happy. I could hear it in the way they talked back.
Then, after only a few days, something went wrong with my power. My voice grew weak, and then it stopped. I could not hear them any more, and they could not hear me.

I thought: now I will fall. I had no engine. I had no wings. I had no one to talk to. Surely I would come crashing down onto the Earth, which was right there, pulling at me every moment. I could feel it, the Earth's pull, never stopping, like a hand on my sleeve.
But I did not crash. I went round. And round. And round.

It took me a long time to understand. I was falling. I had been falling from the very first moment. The Earth was pulling me down, and I was falling towards it, all the time, every second. But I was also moving sideways, fast, eight kilometres every second, and the Earth is round, so as I fell, the ground curved away beneath me. I fell, and missed. Fell, and missed. That is what an orbit is. Not floating. Not resting. Falling, for ever, and never quite arriving.

I was not alone for long. Others came. A small one from India in 1979, then more, then many, then a sky full of them: weather satellites that watched the great spiral cyclones forming over the Bay of Bengal, so people on the coast could be warned, and communication satellites that carried voices from one side of the world to the other. Even the Moon, I realised, was doing what I did. It had been falling round the Earth for four and a half billion years. I was in good company.
Down below, I knew, they had put my picture on the two-rupee note. Children folded me into their pockets and bought sweets with me. I liked to think of that.

I fell round the Earth for nearly seventeen years. More than ninety thousand times round. And all that time, very slowly, the thin, thin air at the top of the sky was rubbing against me, stealing a little of my speed. Each orbit I was a tiny bit lower. Each orbit, the falling won a little more than the missing.

The air grew thick around me and hot, hotter than anything, and I began to glow. I broke apart into a hundred bright sparks streaking across the dark. I do not know who saw me. Maybe nobody. Maybe a fisherman far out at sea, looking up from his boat, or a child on a roof who could not sleep, who saw a shooting star and made a wish.
If you were that child: hello. It was me. I fell for seventeen years, and I never once stopped falling, and that is the only reason I could stay up so long.
story.epiphany: An orbit is not floating. It is a fall that never ends. Gravity pulls a satellite down all the time, but it moves sideways so fast that the round Earth curves away beneath it. The turn comes when the silent, powerless satellite expects to crash and instead understands that it has been falling all along. On the way it sees the line between day and night sweep across India, waking the east almost two hours before the west: the reason for time zones.
ask: Why didn't the satellite Aryabhata fall down when its power stopped?
What did the satellite mean by 'Fell, and missed'?
Why did the satellite see about fifteen sunrises every day?
What made the satellite come down in the end?
The satellite watched morning cross India from Arunachal to Kutch. What does that tell you about time?

ideas.idea: An orbit is falling and missing, for ever.
ideas.more: The Moon, the space station and every satellite are falling towards the Earth all the time. They move sideways so fast that they keep missing. The marble on the plate shows that without the pull, they would go off in a straight line.

ideas.idea: The lines on the globe are partly nature's and partly ours.
ideas.more: The poles, the equator and the tropics come from the Earth's shape, spin and tilt. The prime meridian and time zones were chosen by people at meetings, for practical and political reasons.

ideas.idea: Looking far is looking back in time.
ideas.more: Sunlight is about 8 minutes old when it reaches you. Starlight can be hundreds or thousands of years old. The night sky shows the past.

unknowns: Is there life in the hidden oceans under the ice of Europa, or of Saturn's moon Enceladus? A spacecraft is on its way to Europa to study it, but nobody knows yet.
How can we clean up space debris? Several ideas are being tested, such as nets and harpoons, but nobody has yet cleaned up orbit at a large scale.
How did the Moon form? Most scientists think a Mars-sized world crashed into the young Earth, but the details are still argued about.
